articles.title: CMA CGM raises Asia–Mediterranean rates and announces new surcharges
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced higher Freight All Kind (FAK) rates for shipments from Asia to the Mediterranean and North Africa, alongside new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on other trade routes. The revised FAK rates will apply from November 1 to 14, 2026. Rates for 40-foot containers will reach US$7,100 on shipments to...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced higher Freight All Kind (FAK) rates for shipments from Asia to the Mediterranean and North Africa, alongside new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on other trade routes. The revised FAK rates will apply from November 1 to 14, 2026. Rates for 40-foot containers will reach US$7,100 on shipments to North Africa. The carrier has also announced surcharges for cargo moving from the west coast of South America and from Northern Europe to North Africa. New FAK rates from Asia The new rates cover shipments from major Asian ports to the Western Mediterranean, Adriatic, Eastern Mediterranean, Black Sea and North Africa. Destination 20-foot container 40-foot / 40-foot HC West Mediterranean US$3,900 US$4,900 Adriatic US$4,000 US$5,000 East Mediterranean US$4,200 US$5,200 Black Sea US$4,200 US$5,200 North Africa US$5,300 US$7,100 The rates cover dry, refrigerated, out-of-gauge and paying empty containers. They include basic freight, bunker-related surcharges, Emissions Trading System (ETS) charges and Low Sulphur Surcharges (LSS). However, terminal handling charges, safety and security fees, and other local charges may apply separately. Additional surcharges on other routes From November 1, CMA CGM will introduce a PSS of US$150 per container for dry cargo shipped from the west coast of South America. The surcharge will cover shipments to the eastern coasts of Central America and Mexico, the Caribbean, the Leeward and Windward Islands, and the east coast of South America. It will also apply to cargo bound for Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Separately, CMA CGM will apply a surcharge of €150 per TEU on shipments from Northern Europe to North Africa, starting November 7. The charge will cover all cargo types. Spain and Portugal are excluded from the origin range, while Morocco is excluded from the destination range. The carrier noted that additional bunker, terminal handling and other applicable charges may apply to shipments covered by the new PSS measures.

articles.title: Port of San Diego and Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority sign sister port MOU
articles.summary: The Port of San Diego and the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority of the Philippines have formalised a new sister port partnership, signing a Memorandum of Understanding on October 15 during a celebration attended by SBMA dignitaries and local leaders from the Filipino community. articles.body: The Port of San Diego and the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority of the Philippines have formalised a new sister port partnership, signing a Memorandum of Understanding on October 15 during a celebration attended by SBMA dignitaries and local leaders from the Filipino community. The partnership will enable the two organisations to build trade opportunities, exchange knowledge and collaborate on shared interests across port operations and sustainable development. Subic Bay, located on the west coast of Luzon Island, is a former United States military base repurposed for commercial operations with business lines similar to those of the Port of San Diego, encompassing cargo and cruise operations, shipbuilding facilities, foreign trade zones, hotels, marinas, restaurants, wildlife preserves, recreational centres and an airport. Chair Ann Moore of the Port of San Diego Board of Port Commissioners described the partnership as an extension of the port’s commitment to innovation through strong international relationships, creating opportunities beyond both waterfronts and reinforcing economic resiliency. Commissioner GilAnthony Ungab highlighted the MOU as an avenue for deepening ties with the Philippines and collaborating on import and export cargo opportunities in Asia, alongside sharing best practices in sustainable port development, supply chain resilience and environmental stewardship. Subic Bay is the fourth sister port relationship in the Port of San Diego’s history, following agreements with Sasebo, Japan in 1982, Ensenada, Mexico in 2004 and Nanjing, China in 2012.

articles.title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
articles.summary: In an industry where a position list is a competitive weapon, the question is no longer just how to comply—but where carbon decisions are made and who controls the data behind them, argues Argyris Zafeiropoulos, principal advisor at Resilience & Compliance Advisory. articles.body: Contributions Environment Operations Regulatory Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions? Splash October 20, 2026 0 167 3 minutes read ABS ABS In an industry where a position list is a competitive weapon, the question is no longer just how to comply—but where carbon decisions are made and who controls the data behind them, argues Argyris Zafeiropoulos, principal advisor at Resilience & Compliance Advisory. With the EU Emissions Trading System fully phased into shipping and FuelEU Maritime tightening year by year, carbon is now a line item in every fixture. On a single laden Aframax voyage from the Gulf to Rotterdam, the FuelEU penalty alone climbs to about €246,000 ($276,000) by 2040 — same ship, same route, same fuel. Who pays is a matter of contract. The EU places the obligation on the company holding the ship’s Document of Compliance, and the emissions clauses now in wide use pass it on: under a time charter the charterer typically reimburses it, under a voyage charter the owner prices it into the freight, and a commercial operator carries it on every voyage it fixes. Far less attention goes to a quieter question: where are these carbon decisions actually made, and who can see the data behind them? The reflex of the past decade has been a subscription: upload fleet, fixture and consumption data to a cloud platform and receive a number back. It is convenient. Made by default, it is also a remarkable concession. Position lists, fixture pipelines and consumption curves are competitive assets, and routing them through third-party infrastructure surrenders control at a cost that never appears on an invoice. There is a second cost. Many platforms work as black boxes: they deliver an ETS exposure or a FuelEU penalty, but the methodology stays behind the vendor’s walls. Even scope is a judgement, not a given — whether a Norwegian ore port counts as inside the system, or a transhipment call counts as a port of call at all, can move a leg from 50% to 100% of its emissions. When a broker challenges a break-even, a counterparty disputes an allocation or an auditor asks for justification, “the system said so” is not an answer. In a market where carbon is negotiated line by line, an unauditable calculation is a liability. The alternative rests on three principles. Data should stay under the company’s control by default; what leaves the organisation, and why, should be a conscious choice. Models should be traceable to their sources and anchored in Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 and the IMO framework, not in a formula only the vendor can see. And whoever owns the model owns the decision — which is where the commercial value lies. The real shift is from reporting to deciding. A charterer comparing two similar vessels on the same route may find that the cheaper fixture becomes the more expensive one once ETS and FuelEU are weighed. Discovered after the fixture is concluded, that is a compliance calculation. Understood before it is signed, it is a commercial decision. And deciding means years, not single voyages. On that Aframax, burning conventional very low-sulphur fuel oil, the FuelEU penalty is roughly €19,000 ($21,300) at today’s target, €50,000 ($56,100) at the 2030 target and €246,000 ($276,000) by 2040. A period charter or contract of affreightment signed today is signed across those steps — and the IMO’s draft Net-Zero Framework, due back at MEPC85 in December, could put a global price alongside them. Argyris Zafeiropoulos The arithmetic reaches the cargo too. On that voyage, ETS and FuelEU together come to about €104,000 ($116,600) at an €81 ($91) allowance price — roughly one euro ($1.12) on every tonne of a 100,000-tonne cargo, rising to about €1.36 ($1.53) by 2030. In commodity trades, the choice between CIF and FOB helps decide who absorbs it. Carbon has moved beyond the charter party and into the commodity contract. Third-party platforms are not the problem. Surrendering decision authority to them is. Software is the vehicle, not the authority, and the company that can explain and defend its own numbers stands on firmer ground. Shipping has always rewarded those who control their critical assets — ships, cargo relationships, market intelligence and commercial judgement. As carbon becomes embedded in every voyage, another joins the list: the ability to understand, challenge and defend the carbon number before it becomes a commercial commitment. articles.summary: The Trump administration is authorizing the sale of sanctioned oil tankers in an effort to allow the vessels to start legitimately shipping crude, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said.

REUTERS/Khalil Ashawi By Ari Natter and Annmarie Hordern (Bloomberg) — The Trump administration is authorizing the sale of sanctioned oil tankers in an effort to allow the vessels to start legitimately shipping crude, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. The US government is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use the ships to transport non-sanctioned oil, Wright said Monday at a Citadel Securities event in New York. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’ ” Wright said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore.” Wright’s comments represent the first detailed public explanation from the Trump administration about turning to sanctioned tankers as it seeks to expand the number of ships available to transport crude and boost supply disrupted by the war in Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump administration is undertaking an approval process to grant ships legitimate status, Wright said. He rejected the idea that the US was simply removing sanctions from tankers that carried crude from nations such as Russia or Iran. “We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers,” Wright said. “There is no removing of sanctions.” The move comes as Republicans in the US confront voters who are concerned about higher fuel costs weeks before midterm elections. Gasoline and diesel prices surged following the Mideast conflict adding a pain point for voters already worried about affordability. Wright estimated that there are about 1,600 vessels in the global “dark fleet” of sanctioned tankers. The Trump administration’s effort to convert those into lawful ships could ultimately add “dozens” or even “hundreds” of tankers to the legitimate fleet, he said. The perils of transporting oil through the strait have sent shipping fees skyrocketing. Moving oil from the Persian Gulf to East Asia costs more than six times as much as it did prior to the conflict. More than 40% of the world’s fleet of about 850 very large crude carriers are now either in the Persian Gulf or within a couple of days sailing time from it, according to Signal Ocean, a shipping data provider. In addition, Wright said during the wide-ranging interview that part of the reason the Trump administration agreed to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release the country’s diesel supplies into global markets in a widely criticized move was to provide an incentive for the Kremlin to end the war with Ukraine. “If you can produce more diesel than you consume, you can export it to the world. Well, what’s their route to do that? They can they can end the conflict in Ukraine,” Wright said. “That would be a real plus. They could get an energy ceasefire with the Ukrainians and fix their refineries, or they can reduce their consumption of diesel for war fighting activities. So if they change their behavior, and all of these are steps towards peace in the conflict, and you have surplus diesel, where you can export it to the world.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The El Niño impact on shipping is one to consider, when considering potential 2027 freight disruptions. Timing matters as...
articles.body: Shipping: The El Niño Effect in Hellenic Shipping News 20/10/2026 T he El Niño impact on shipping is one to consider, when considering potential 2027 freight disruptions. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “with El Niño now established and forecasters pointing to a strong event, the question for shipping is where it affects freight first. Timing matters as much as strength: the largest effects on crops, water levels and trade usually arrive in the first half of the following year, which places the main freight impact in 2027. El Niño is a dynamic disruption and its effects vary by region. Drier conditions are expected across Central America, including the Panama Canal watershed, while the impact on Brazil is different by region, with drier conditions in the central and northern grain producing states. Argentina and the southern United States, by contrast, tend to receive more rain. India, Southeast Asia and Australia are set to face droughts”. Source: Intermodal shipbroker According to Mr. Vasilis Fousekis, Research Analyst with Intermodal, “for dry bulk, the canal is the most direct link. The Panama Canal Authority, after cutting daily transits to 32 in September – only the second such reduction in history, eased restrictions following late-September rain. The relief, though, may not last. Panama’s meteorological institute expects the dry season to begin as early as the second half of November, cutting into what is normally the wettest month, when Gatun Lake is replenished. The Authority projects an average of 29.5 crossings a day over the coming fiscal year. It is also auctioning long term slots for the older Panamax locks for the first time, covering January to early April 2027. Rerouting is already visible, as deviation through the Strait of Magellan rose sharply in August and September, supporting Panamax and Kamsarmax utilisation, even when volumes are flat”. “In coal, El Niño brings drought to Southeast Asia, reducing hydropower output, and increasing coal burn, notably in India and Vietnam, contributing to the shift to coal as a source of energy, in a period of high natural gas prices. However, seaborne trade is more selective. India and China are expected to import less thermal coal this year, as they draw on high domestic stocks, impacting total seaborne thermal volumes, with growth concentrated on short-haul Southeast Asian routes, such as Indonesia or Australia to Vietnam, limiting the tonne-mile gain”, Mr. Fousekis said. Similarly, “in grains, El Niño is expected to affect Brazil’s 2026/27 crop mainly through irregular rainfall in central and northern Brazil, while the south faces excess rain. The key risk lies between November and January, when dry spells and heat could reduce soybean yields in Mato Grosso and the northern states, leaving the outlook for a record harvest skewed to the downside. Any delay to the soybean cycle would also push second-crop corn planting beyond its ideal window, threatening yields and Brazil’s corn exports in the second half of 2027. Some offset in South American grain trade may come from Argentina, where favorable rainfall is set to support export volumes. The United States stands to benefit, as a record soybean crop and the second-largest corn crop on record leave it well placed to fill the gap, with a longer export window into Asia in early 2027 and stronger demand for its corn later in the year. The constraint is logistics rather than supply, as Panama Canal restrictions during the dry season would limit how much of this opportunity US exporters can capture”, he noted. Source: Intermodal shipbroker Intermodal’s analyst also commented that “drought in the Central American Dry Corridor could also lift short-haul grain imports from the US Gulf, a modest gain for Handysize and Supramax owners. In Australia, a dry spring is already reducing wheat yields in the eastern states as the harvest begins, although large carry-in stocks could cushion exports, including shipments to China. Effects of the phenomenon extend as well beyond dry bulk, with a notable example being Indonesian palm oil. Prolonged drought and severe wildfires are likely to lower exports, pushing importers towards more distant vegetable oil origins and lengthening hauls for product tanker owners. Overall, El Niño effects on shipping spread through reshuffling of logistics and trade flows rather than through large swings in volumes, as also past events showed. Panama is the clearest channel for dry bulk and the most likely to tighten into early 2027, while other important impacts include potential for uplift in thermal coal demand due to declining hydropower and shifts in seaborne grain trade patterns”, he concldued. articles.body: How Conflict in the Middle East is Impacting Maritime in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 M iddle Eastern buyers have been far more active in the Tanker S&P market over the past quarter. Between July 1 and Oct. 5, they made 34 Tanker purchases, up from 21 in the same period last year, an increase of more than 60%. The rise is concentrated at the top end of the fleet. VLCC purchases climbed from 1 to 19, and Suezmax purchases from 2 to 7. Notable recent sales include the Vadin (308,000 DWT, Aug 2006, Mitsui Ichihara) that sold to Onex DMXX for USD 117 mil, adding to the additional seven VLCCs and Suezmaxes purchased by the company since the start of September. The Strait of Hormuz crisis is the clear driver of the purchase activity. Transit volumes through the Strait fell sharply after the ceasefire collapsed in early July, and the alternatives have come under pressure too. Drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and Houthi threats around Bab el-Mandeb narrowed the options for moving Middle Eastern crude. As a result, fewer open market owners are willing to trade in the Gulf, and for producers and regional trading houses, buying tonnage outright has become a way of securing the ability to keep crude and money moving. There is a sellers angle too. For risk averse owners who will not trade in the region themselves, selling at elevated values offers a way to capture some of the gains created by the Middle East Gulf risk and rate environment, taking part in an extreme market without taking on the exposure. Positioning is key, with premiums most pronounced where delivery into the Gulf is a firm requirement. Earnings have added to the pull, with VLCC rates on the Middle East Gulf to China route pushing past 1,300,000 USD/day for the first time. Sale prices have followed, reaching record levels. For example, 15 YO VLCCs of 310,000 DWT have increased by 163.45% year-on-year from USD 55 mil to USD 144.9 mil. Whether these levels hold beyond this narrow pool of buyers will depend largely on how the disruption develops. Onex DMCC’s buying spree amid tight tonnage supply By Rebecca Galanopoulos Onex DMCC’s appetite has continued beyond the Pinios deal, with the trading house now linked to six VLCC and Suezmax purchases in recent weeks. Another VLCC, the Ashoka (302,600 DWT, Mar 2010, Universal), has also changed hands to Middle Eastern buyers at USD 130 mil. The deals rank among the highest ever seen for VLCC tonnage and highlight the breadth of regional demand for immediately available tonnage. Onex’s willingness to pay up for prompt tonnage has become a driving force behind current values, setting a new reference point for future sales. That demand coincides with VLCC earnings surging to unprecedented levels, with rates on the benchmark Middle East Gulf to China route pushing past 1,000,000 USD /day for the first time. The move follows drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which had been carrying a significant share of the kingdom’s crude exports to the Red Sea as an alternative to the still-disrupted Strait of Hormuz. With that bypass route now compromised, the pool of viable options for moving Middle Eastern crude has narrowed further, adding fresh upward pressure to an already tight Tanker market. VLCC sale values surge as market strains to keep oil flowing out of Middle East By Rebecca Galanopoulos Middle Eastern oil majors have shown growing interest in VLCC purchases recently, with S&P activity increasingly shaped by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The VLCC Pinios (306,000 DWT, Feb 2026, Hengli), delivered to Dynacom earlier this year, has reportedly been resold to UAE based Onex DMCC for nearly USD 200 mil, a record price for a resale. Positioning is vital in this market: delivery to Fujairah alone is estimated to be worth around USD 10 mil to Onex, with the price also reflecting a discount tied to the vessel’s yard. This premium is driven by strong spot charter earnings, the risk attached to Strait of Hormuz transits, and the priority of enabling Iraqi oil to leave the Gulf. Premiums of this scale appear most pronounced where delivery into the Gulf is a firm requirement, reflecting how few owners remain willing to trade in the area. Whether such levels hold for wider market sales rather than this narrow pool of national buyers remains to be seen. UAE-based ADNOC Logistics has acquired nine VLCCs since late June, worth around USD 1.1 bil in total, a move that points to a Middle East producer strengthening its own Tanker fleet as fewer open market vessels are willing to face the risk of trading in the Gulf. For national oil companies, owning tonnage outright has become less a commercial decision and more a means of securing tonnage so that crude and money can keep moving. Could the Middle East crisis turn positive for MRs this fall? By Thomas Zwick Roughly 70 LR2s, equivalent to 154 MR2s in dwt terms, have reportedly dirtied up so far this year, as the crude market considerably outperformed the oil products market. The predominant market for product carrying LR2s is out of the Middle East Gulf, but with the region’s cargo availability constrained and waters risky, earnings potential for LR2s should have logically been deteriorating. However, they have held up remarkably well since the conflict began in late February. The LR2s that remained in clean trade have recently benefited from the roughly 70 vessels that switched to dirty, according to TORM’s most recent earnings call, tightening the market for larger product tankers over the past couple of weeks. While the broader market is currently supported by inefficiencies stemming from the Middle East conflict and the ongoing ship-to-ship operations it has triggered, a scenario where the Strait of Hormuz becomes increasingly viable as a safe transit route could see regional refineries offer a growing volume of LR2 cargoes. If that materializes, the pool of available LR2s may prove limited or poorly positioned geographically to absorb the demand rebound, creating a potential tailwind for MRs, whose availability has risen and rates have been under pressure lately. The net effect could be a new, if temporary, market opening for medium-sized vessels in the region, arriving just as MR2s typically exit a subdued summer and head into the stronger market ahead of winter. Six months into disruption, why aren’t global gas prices skyrocketing? By Jarl Milford We are in the sixth month of vessel disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, and despite weekly hints of a possible resolution to the conflict, vessel activity remains at a standstill. According to AIS tracking, larger-size LNG vessels out of Qatar have declined 93% on average during the conflict compared to the 2025 monthly average. Given the circumstances, vessels have managed to sail through the strait with their AIS turned off as a precautionary measure to avoid being targeted, but even accounting for this, the disruption’s impact is significant. Why then haven’t global gas prices gone through the roof? JKM prices have doubled since the conflict began but remain well below the levels seen during the 2022 gas shock. The picture is, of course, shaped by several factors, including inventory draws, demand rationing, and increased coal fired generation. But the factor that stands out most is the surge in North American export volumes: US LNG exports are up 22% YTD, according to customs data. Canada, which only began LNG exports in mid-2025, has already shipped 5.5 Mt in the first of the year, more than double its full-year 2025 total of 2.3 Mt. Much of this growth comes from new LNG capacity, particularly Golden Pass and LNG Canada, both ramping up this year. Combined, this additional North American supply has offset a meaningful share of the lost Qatari volumes, tempering what could otherwise have been a much sharper price spike. The outlook for the second half of the year remains uncertain given the unresolved Middle East situation. While the gas market has proven resilient so far, if the disruption drags on, we could see conditions tighten heading into winter. Bab el-Mandeb Transits Slide as Risks Mount By Rebecca Galanopoulos Bab el-Mandeb Strait transits fell by around a third week-on-week, according to Veson Nautical’s VesselsValue trade data, from the week of 16-22 July to the week of 23-29 July, amid continued Houthi threats, including a Saudi-flagged Tanker that multiple sources reported was struck on 28 July. All three vessels involved in the earlier reroute were VLCCs, which turned back toward the Suez Canal rather than continue through Bab el-Mandeb in the days after the blockade declaration. The decline follows major insurers suspending war-risk cargo cover for Saudi-linked vessels, prompting some operators to avoid direct calls at Saudi Red Sea ports while others bypass the Red Sea entirely in favour of the Cape of Good Hope, despite the considerably longer voyage. Bab el-Mandeb still carries a meaningfully larger share of global trade than the effectively closed Strait of Hormuz, as it remains the primary gateway linking the Suez Canal to Asia-Europe Container flows as well as continued Saudi crude exports, though volumes are down from pre-crisis norms. The route remains functional but increasingly strained, standing in contrast to Hormuz’s near-total shutdown. Bab al-Mandeb Closes, Hormuz Still Falling: Tanker Data Update By Rebecca Galanopoulos On 20 July, Houthi forces declared a full maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia, closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait to vessels servicing Saudi ports. Following this move, Tanker Xin Long Yang, a Chinese VLCC carrying Saudi crude, turned back towards Suez rather than cross the Yemeni border, and two more Tankers followed suit. Within days, the Houthis said they had gone further, striking two Saudi-flagged Tankers.with missiles and drones and causing fires The Bab al-Mandeb Strait carries around 7% of global oil output. The Strait of Hormuz has been under severe strain since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February, and our own transit data below shows it accelerating towards a halt rather than recovering, down around 95% since the ceasefire collapsed in early July. A sustained Bab al-Mandeb shutdown would compound that; the two chokepoints could remove a significant volume of the world’s oil and gas supply. While the two straits are separate, they have become increasingly linked, with Saudi Arabia routing up to 7mbd of crude oil via the Red Sea to work around the Hormuz disruption. Taking a look at VesselsValue trade data, transit volumes for the Strait of Hormuz have continued falling across the last three weeks amid the back-and-forth policies. Tanker and LNG volumes transiting the strait were down around 62% from the Monday the ceasefire broke down to the following Monday. They then fell a further 87% into this Monday, leaving transit volume down around 95% versus the pre-breakdown baseline overall, enough to suggest a real pause in movement rather than simply week-week variation. The sharpest day-to-day swings seen in the days immediately after the ceasefire broke down have eased since, though volumes are still suppressed relative to the pre-breakdown baseline. Transit dates are marked by first known position past the tripwire, a fixed line drawn using VesselsValue Trade search across the strait that flags a transit once a vessel reappears on the far side, consistent with the tripwire search logic. Since vessels typically go dark crossing the strait, it is worth flagging that this likely lags actual transits somewhat, so current-week figures may still tick up as more positions resolve. TC rates moved only modestly week on week, continuing the gentle drift seen since the announcement and reversal rather than reacting freshly to it, consistent with a market that had already priced in Gulf risk. TC rates have risen week-on-week for most sectors with VLCCs up from 110,139 USD/day to 113,310 USD/day, an increase of c. 3%. Suezmaxes were also up c.3%, while Afras dipped slightly. Product Tankers were flatter and LR1 and MR1 each nudged up roughly 1%. VLCC’s current week average is now running about 48% above the one year average of 76,485 USD/day. Oil prices have moved on the Red Sea news: Following 13 consecutive nights of US and Iranian strikes in the Middle East conflict, oil prices broke 100 USD/bbl on Thursday for the first time since May. The key signals to watch: whether the Houthis follow through with further attacks beyond Encelia and Layla, if any more Tankers reroute away from Bab al-Mandeb entirely, and whether transit volumes and TC rates in the Hormuz data above start reflecting this second chokepoint risk on top of the existing Iran-related disruption. articles.title: Hydrogen sulphide: The hidden danger outside enclosed spaces
articles.summary: A review of fatal incidents submitted to the IMO shows that many seafarers were overcome by H₂S while carrying out routine maintenance and inspection activities outside enclosed spaces. Crew members have collapsed while opening tank manholes, dismantling pumps and pipelines, working near tank vents, and attempting to...
articles.body: Hydrogen sulphide: The hidden danger outside enclosed spaces in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 20/10/2026 A review of fatal incidents submitted to the IMO shows that many seafarers were overcome by H₂S while carrying out routine maintenance and inspection activities outside enclosed spaces. Crew members have collapsed while opening tank manholes, dismantling pumps and pipelines, working near tank vents, and attempting to rescue colleagues. In many of these incidents, the victims had no intention of entering a tank. The findings highlight an important safety message: H₂S should not be viewed solely as an enclosed-space entry hazard. It is also a release hazard. Personnel can be exposed during everyday shipboard operations whenever a contaminated system is opened, disturbed or ventilated. More than half of fatalities happened outside According to IMO document CCC 12/INF.20 (10 July 2026), at least 29 of 56 identified H₂S-related fatalities occurred outside enclosed spaces. The victims were carrying out routine tasks when a sudden release of H₂S caused immediate collapse. These findings challenge the traditional perception that H₂S fatalities are primarily linked to enclosed-space entry. A hazardous gas release can also occur during normal shipboard operations, as the following case study illustrates. Case study: fatal exposure while opening a bilge water tank Before cleaning a bilge water tank on a drillship, a Second Engineer (2/E) and a Motorman opened the tank access hatch to allow for ventilation. Moments later, as he was climbing away from the hatch, the 2/E suddenly collapsed, and both men fell into the tank. Tragically, despite rescue efforts, both men lost their lives. The investigation found that the tank contained oily water and residue deposits capable of generating H₂S. Opening the hatch likely released accumulated gas into the surrounding pump room, exposing the workers before any tank entry had begun. The incident highlights a crucial point: simply opening a tank can release a potentially fatal concentration of H₂S. What is H₂S knockdown? H₂S knockdown refers to the sudden collapse and loss of consciousness that can occur following exposure to very high concentrations of hydrogen sulphide. H₂S is a colourless, highly toxic, and flammable gas. It is heavier than air and tends to accumulate in low-lying areas such as tank bottoms, bilges, pits, and poorly ventilated spaces. While low concentrations may produce the characteristic smell of rotten eggs, this odour cannot be relied upon as a warning. Exposure can rapidly paralyse the sense of smell, leaving individuals unaware that concentrations are increasing. At concentrations of approximately 700-1,000 ppm, a person may collapse after only a few breaths. Respiratory paralysis and death can occur within minutes. In such situations, portable gas detectors may provide little practical warning if the release is sudden or exceeds the detector’s measuring range. How does H₂S develop? H₂S is commonly generated when organic or oil-containing materials decompose under oxygen-deficient conditions. On board vessels, the combination of seawater and organic or oily residues can create ideal conditions for sulphate-reducing bacteria to produce H₂S. Potential sources include: • Oily slops and sludge • Sewage and grey-water systems • Fuel oil residues • Food waste and organic wash water • Bilges and bilge holding tanks • Cargo residues • Contaminated ballast tanks Even small quantities of seawater mixed with these materials can generate significant concentrations of H₂S. Biodegradable detergents and nutrient-rich wastes may further accelerate the process. A particular challenge is that H₂S may remain dissolved within liquids and only be released when conditions change, such as when a tank is opened, contents are agitated or pumped, tank washing begins or pressure conditions change. As a result, a space that appears safe may suddenly release a concentrated cloud of gas during an otherwise routine operation. Preventing H₂S knockdown The first control is to recognize tank opening, opening a pump or a pipe, and disturbance of residues as potential toxic-gas release operations. The risk assessment should address both the source space and the surrounding or connected space. • Assess before opening: Check the space’s history and contents, including previous storage of sewage, grey water, oily water, slops, cargo residues, seawater and cleaning chemicals. Consider duration of storage, temperature, agitation and whether the space can be sampled through a closed-system point. No opening or venting should proceed until the assessment is complete and controls are in place. • Consider the release path of the gas: Determine where gas could move when pressure is released or ventilation begins. Keep personnel away from the likely release path, low points and restricted escape routes. If an opening must be cracked for testing, it should be done incrementally from a safe position, with monitoring and emergency arrangements ready. • Test and continue testing: Use a suitable, calibrated multigas detector capable of measuring H₂S, oxygen and flammable gases, plus any other gases identified by the assessment. Test at representative levels and locations. Repeat testing after washing, pumping, agitation, ventilation changes or any interruption that could alter the atmosphere. However, gas testing alone should not be relied upon as the sole safeguard. A sudden release of highly concentrated H₂S may occur too rapidly for a standard detector to provide effective warning, and concentrations capable of causing knockdown may exceed the measuring range of typical shipboard instruments. The possibility of a sudden release should therefore always be considered before opening a manhole, flange, valve or other containment. • Control tank contents: Minimise unnecessary storage of oily water and other nutrient-rich mixtures. Review drainage pathways so galley, sanitary or other nutrient-bearing wastes do not enter oily-water systems. Use fresh water for cleaning where practicable, manage biodegradable detergents carefully, and avoid creating stagnant, anaerobic conditions. • Prepare for rescue without creating more victims: A person affected by H₂S may collapse without warning. No one should rush into a contaminated or untested area. Rescue must follow the vessel’s emergency arrangements and use suitable respiratory protection, trained personnel, and retrieval equipment. Connected spaces must also be treated as potentially hazardous. Source: Gard, https://www.gard.no/en/insights/hydrogen-sulphide-the-hidden-danger-outside-enclosed-spaces/ 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Crew members have collapsed while opening tank manholes, dismantling pumps and pipelines, working near tank vents, and attempting to rescue colleagues.
In many of these incidents, the victims had no intention of entering a tank.
The findings highlight an important safety message: H₂S should not be viewed solely as an enclosed-space entry hazard.

articles.title: How Ports Can Become Catalysts For The Blue Economy
articles.summary: Valued at between $2.6 and $5.1 trillion, the ocean economy supports billions of livelihoods and carries more than 80% of global trade by volume. However, its continued expansion will increasingly intersect with natural ecosystems and local communities. The global port infrastructure market is forecast to grow by...
articles.body: How Ports Can Become Catalysts For The Blue Economy in Port News 20/10/2026 V alued at between $2.6 and $5.1 trillion, the ocean economy supports billions of livelihoods and carries more than 80% of global trade by volume. However, its continued expansion will increasingly intersect with natural ecosystems and local communities. The global port infrastructure market is forecast to grow by nearly 70%, from $164.5 billion in 2023 to $278.3 billion by 2032. Asia-Pacific dominates the market, capturing an impressive 45% share. This dominance can be attributed to the presence of major global manufacturing hubs, and ports in developing Asian economies handled 60% of global container port traffic in 2024. India alone in just 10 years has almost doubled the number of containers passing through its ports, and its strategic Sagarmala project, dating back to the beginning of this growth, provides a strong foundation to support continued expansion of the port ecosystem. So how can we leverage these trade hubs to become key enablers of the “blue economy”? How global risks like climate change impact ports As highlighted in the World Economic Forum’s Global Risks Report 2026, long-term risks to Earth systems, society and the economy are dominated by the impact of climate change, with extreme weather events, biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse, and critical change to Earth systems ranked among the most severe. These risks are already playing out in ports, which face a series of climate and nature hazards and growing exposure to operational disruptions. In Europe, port operational challenges linked to climate change rose from 41% in 2018 to 69% in 2025, while in Asia, many major ports are highly exposed to sea-level rise, storms and flooding. Maritime decarbonization, both on land and at sea, can help mitigate the impact of risks such as climate change by lowering emissions – the first driver of nature loss. There are economic benefits too – future-proofing ports to support this transition could unlock more than $54 billion in cumulative value by 2030. But this transition requires action and sustained investment. Ports face dual challenge of decarbonization and resilience The decarbonization of the maritime industry is being driven in large part by the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) target to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. This planned transition to alternative fuels such as green methanol, green ammonia and synthetic e-fuels will require significant infrastructure development and upgrades. As of 2025, global retrofit capacity was estimated at roughly 465 vessels annually, against a projected peak need of more than 1,000 conversions per year. So new and retrofitted bunkering facilities will be needed, transition-ready vessels must be built and existing fleets upgraded, while shipyard capacity, particularly for retrofits, will need to scale rapidly. The scale of investment required to meet the IMO 2050 target is estimated at $1-1.4 trillion, with about 87% of that investment directed to land-side infrastructure and 13% to ships. Nature and people as strategic assets for resilience A daunting figure but with new fuels come new skills – those needed to handle them safely at sea and ashore, from the ship’s tanks to the terminals that serve them. The transition requires creating safer, more resilient and inclusive jobs and communities, and developing the skills needed to strengthen transition capacity while placing health and safety at the heart of strategy and operations. The maritime sector already directly employs 30 million people and indirectly benefits 90 million jobs, and the shift to scalable zero emission marine fuels could create up to 4 million jobs across the energy supply chain by 2050. Ports are key as, onshore, they provide the infrastructure needed to produce, store and bunker alternative fuels, build and retrofit vessels and enable green corridors, while, at sea, their transformation is essential for vessels to access the future fuel mix. Maritime decarbonization also presents an opportunity to responsibly deploy infrastructure and transform business models by positioning nature, water and people as strategic assets for resilience, while recognizing nature as cost-effective protective infrastructure when incorporated with nature-based solutions, nature-inclusive design, and secure and circular water and waste systems. Shaping the blue future of maritime hubs Given the long lifespan of port and energy infrastructure, responsible decisions made today will shape the resilience and competitiveness of maritime hubs for decades. The maritime fuel transition offers an opportunity to upgrade existing infrastructure and develop new greenfield projects using this investment cycle responsibly, while incorporating nature and people as critical infrastructure and factor of resilience across the port ecosystem. At the same time, organizations will also need to better integrate their nature-positive and net zero strategies as tackling carbon emissions and nature loss are interdependent imperatives. Such considerations will need to be embedded into long-term strategy, day-to-day operations and investment decisions. WEF’s Regenerative Blue Economy: Pathways to Prosperity report shows that many organizations are already beginning this shift, but scaling it will depend on demonstrating commercial viability, strengthening the business case and moving from individual projects and pilots to more systemic adoption. The port ecosystem as a strategic platform Scaling decarbonization efforts will also depend on how much companies will be able to collaborate with other stakeholders. The port ecosystem is highly interdependent, but often institutionally fragmented. As a result, risks can be recognized but not fully owned, investments delayed or duplicated, incentives misaligned, and resilience measures implemented only partially rather than systemically. Addressing these challenges requires a collaborative, system-wide effort. Over five years, the Transitioning Industrial Clusters (TIC) initiative has brought together 40-plus active industrial clusters with the aim of developing a shared vision and strengthening collaboration among organizations located in the same industrial area. Meanwhile, the Accelerating Critical Transformation for the Ocean (ACT Ocean) initiative works across sectors to advance solutions for a healthy ocean and thriving economy and help shape the future of the ocean as a strategic business issue. Accelerating Critical Transformation for Ports (ACT Ports) is the port workstream under these two initiatives. Together, these World Economic Forum initiatives help drive shared economic growth and job creation, while reducing emissions and supporting environmental stewardship. They also seek to catalyse collaboration between co-located companies to accelerate new technology deployment, enhance competitiveness and drive sustainable long-term growth, thereby unlocking benefits for nature, people and the economy. How Asia can lead on the maritime transition The benefits of maritime decarbonization are multi-fold but the opportunity is particularly significant in Asia, where the scale and pace of port and industrial growth mean that decisions taken today will shape maritime infrastructure for decades. Embedding nature, people are resilient and responsible investments decisions from the outset to turn these trade hubs into gateways to the blue economy. If done successfully, the region will be well placed to lead the next generation of competitive, resilient and sustainable maritime ecosystems – for the benefit of all. articles.title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
articles.summary: InterManager has called for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety after its latest research highlighted persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. articles.body: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 InterManager has called for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety after its latest research highlighted persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. The organisation has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, across tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. Its latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. Over 900 respondents highlighted overly complex paperwork, inadequate time and manpower, commercial pressure, insufficient practical training and a reluctance to address underlying causes. The survey also highlights concerns that inspections can focus on superficial compliance rather than the effectiveness of actual safety practices. It also identifies opportunities to make greater use of real-time gas sensors, wearable technology, digital permits, hands-free communications and unmanned inspection tools to reduce human exposure. The organisation says its latest seafarer research points to two clear priorities. The need for continuous professional development, rather than one-off training, and for seafarers to be more directly engaged in the systems, ships and resources they are expected to operate safely. InterManager Secretary General Capt Kuba Szymanski Current enclosed space training is often concentrated around a single exercise when people commence their careers. InterManager says this must now be enhanced to deliver competence, rather than just training, particularly as enclosed space entry training is being considered as part of the current review of STW requirements, with the International Chamber of Shipping leading industry input. InterManager will explore the survey findings and wider enclosed space safety concerns during a webinar, run in conjunction with The Nautical Institute, on 27 October 2026 at 10am GMT. The webinar will bring together industry experts, Captain Pradeep Chawla, CEO of Marie Pals, Captain Garry Hallett from InterManager and Richard Cowburn, human factors specialist, to discuss where the industry stands now on enclosed space safety, how seafarers and shore-based stakeholders feel about current practice, and what practical action is needed next. The session will be moderated by David Patrirko FNI, Director of Projects at The Nautical Institute and aims to inform, educate and engage the industry by sharing the research findings, discussing operational realities and encouraging wider debate on how enclosed space deaths can be prevented. Captain Kuba Szymanski, Secretary General of InterManager, comments: “Enclosed spaces have been killing seafarers for decades. The industry does not need more paperwork for the sake of paperwork, it needs practical measures that work onboard. If a procedure cannot realistically be completed with the time, people and equipment available, then we need to question the system, not blame the seafarer.” InterManager says training should place greater emphasis on how enclosed space entry should be carried out safely in real operational conditions, supported by regular drills, refresher training, effective gas detection and robust rescue arrangements. It is also calling for greater attention to ship design, including reducing the need for enclosed space entry through better equipment positioning, improved coatings and more durable pipework. It also criticises poor industry data sharing and inconsistencies in accident investigation, warning that lessons cannot be learned effectively if information is delayed, incomplete or withheld. Captain Szymanski adds: “We already know many of the factors behind these accidents. What is missing is consistent action. The priority now must be simpler procedures, better training, stronger leadership, improved ship design and far greater sharing of accident data. Enclosed space deaths are not inevitable. The industry has the knowledge to prevent them so why isn’t it doing it already?” Source: InterManager 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
articles.summary: Shipping companies need to pay as much attention to managing crew turnover as they do to retaining seafarers if they are to maintain safe and efficient vessel operations, according to Henrik Jensen, founder and CEO of Danica Crewing Specialists. Speaking ahead of this week’s Crew Connect Global 2026 in Manila (20-22...
articles.body: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention in International Shipping News 20/10/2026 Shipping companies need to pay as much attention to managing crew turnover as they do to retaining seafarers if they are to maintain safe and efficient vessel operations, according to Henrik Jensen, founder and CEO of Danica Crewing Specialists. Speaking ahead of this week’s Crew Connect Global 2026 in Manila (20-22 October), Mr Jensen warned that while retaining experienced seafarers remains a priority, changing attitudes towards employment mean shipowners and managers must accept that some crew turnover is inevitable and be better prepared to manage it. “Having a stable crew pool makes a significant difference to the safe and efficient operation of a vessel. Experienced crews who know the ship, its equipment and each other are less likely to make mistakes, helping prevent accidents, damage and costly disruption,” he said. “Shipping companies understandably invest heavily in retention, but even those offering excellent employment conditions will lose crew members. We also need to think about how we manage these changes when they happen.” Mr Jensen explained that traditional retention strategies, including competitive salaries, bonuses, insurance, pensions and promotion opportunities, have largely been built around the expectations of older generations, who tend to value stability and long-term employment. However, younger seafarers are often more willing to explore new opportunities, even when satisfied with their existing conditions, a trend he believes will become more significant as they progress through the ranks. “Younger people are generally more open to trying something different. With competition for skilled workers across many industries, we cannot expect everyone to stay with the same employer indefinitely,” he explained. Henrik Jensen Mr Jensen believes shipping companies should focus on making it easier for new crew members to familiarise themselves with onboard equipment, procedures and working practices. “Every time something goes wrong onboard, there is a tendency to introduce another procedure or checklist. Over the years, these requirements build up and systems become increasingly complicated, leaving new crew members with an enormous amount of information to absorb, often without enough time to do so properly.” He recommends reviewing safety and quality management procedures at least annually to remove outdated or unnecessary requirements, while ensuring familiarisation focuses on the practical instructions relevant to each seafarer’s role. Digital systems and artificial intelligence could also help crew members find and understand relevant procedures more quickly, while greater standardisation of equipment and regulations would make moving between vessels easier. Mr Jensen pointed to differences between manufacturers’ ECDIS systems as an example of unnecessary complexity. “We should be making it easier for people to join a new vessel and become familiar with its systems without compromising safety,” he said. “Of course, we must continue doing everything we can to retain good seafarers, but we also need to accept that some turnover is unavoidable. If we want safe and efficiently operated vessels, we need to manage both retention and the movement of crew. The two must go hand in hand.” Source: Danica Shipping 2026-10-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: WinGD has recorded the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol fuel engine platform on ethanol fuel, following a successful bunkering and voyage in the US. The 9,000 TEU container ship Tangier Maersk, owned by the Maersk shipping line, successfully sailed from Houston to New York on ethanol fuel. The...
articles.body: Ethanol debut for WinGD as Maersk vessel makes landmark US bunkering and voyage in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 20/10/2026 WinGD has recorded the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol fuel engine platform on ethanol fuel, following a successful bunkering and voyage in the US. The 9,000 TEU container ship Tangier Maersk, owned by the Maersk shipping line, successfully sailed from Houston to New York on ethanol fuel. The vessel took on the bunker at the Port of Houston in late September, with the world’s largest bioethanol producer POET supplying fuel for the WinGD X82DF-Mengine powering the vessel. The occasion marked the first marine bunkering of a 100% bioethanol blend in the US, and the first ever in-service bunkering of ethanol to a WinGD engine. As well as highlighting the increasing availability of bioethanol to marine markets – POET alone produces 3 billion gallons a year across 35 sites – the sailing marks a milestone in the operational record of WinGD’s alcohol fuel engine platform. The first X-DF-M/E engine capable of using methanol entered service in 2025, with multi-alcohol fuel capability added this year – enabling both methanol and ethanol fuel to be used on six mid-sized sister vessels ordered by Maersk. Tangier Maersk at the Port of Mobile, Alabama. (Image credit: Alabama Port Authority) WinGD Vice President Research & Development Sebastian Hensel said: “The use of bioethanol as a marine fuel is a natural progression for WinGD after successful operating experience with methanol using the same engine platform. This debut, a result of the strong momentum of Maersk in validating the use of this cost-effective low-carbon fuel, enabled us to confirm important operational and safety functions. This landmark will give added confidence to ship operators considering bioethanol as an emerging route to maritime decarbonisation.” Sebastian Hensel, Director R&D, WinGD The successful bunkering operation was the result of strong collaboration between several partners, with Maersk providing the vessel, Kirby Corporation providing fuel transportation and bunkering, and the Port of Houston overseeing port coordination. The US Coast Guard also supported the project by verifying that regulatory requirements to conduct the bunkering operation had been met. Emma Mazhari, Maersk’s Vice President Energy Markets said: “Bioethanol is a scalable, lower-emission fuel option that can offer greater flexibility in how the maritime industry approaches its transition to lower-carbon fuels. This operation is an important step in exploring how bioethanol can be incorporated into marine fuel supply chains.” The chemical similarities between methanol and ethanol mean that both can be used in WinGD’s X-DF-M/E engines, with injection optimised for either fuel or for similar performance with both fuels. This flexibility means that operators can switch between the two fuels in the same engine depending on greenhouse gas emissions reduction requirements, cost and availability – delivering a more cost-effective transition towards net-zero emissions from international shipping. articles.body: Hambantota International Port has delivered 167,569 vehicles across the March to December 2025 period and through September 2026, supporting vehicle importers through periods of increased demand and supply chain disruption. Of the total, 86,389 vehicles were delivered between March and December 2025, comprising 30,809 brand new and 55,580 used vehicles, with a further 81,180 vehicles delivered through September 2026, including 25,018 brand new and 56,162 used units. HIPG responded to several operational challenges during the period, including demurrage waivers and concessions during the period of vehicle import restrictions when customers’ vehicles remained at the port for extended periods. More recently, disruptions to vehicle transhipment through the Gulf region prompted HIPG to introduce a storage cap mechanism for affected vehicles, helping manage storage costs and providing customers with greater cost predictability during the disruption period. The Vehicle Importers’ Association of Lanka, representing more than 450 members across Sri Lanka including established companies and micro, small and medium enterprises, recognised HIPG’s responsiveness, operational flexibility and practical support in addressing challenges faced by its members. HIPG CEO Wilson Qu described the close dialogue with VIAL as essential to understanding customers’ operational needs and responding effectively as market conditions change, framing the relationship as reflective of the port’s commitment to efficient vehicle handling and supply chain continuity. General Manager Commercial and Marketing Bindu Ranasinghe highlighted the focus on helping customers manage costs through practical measures while building long-term trust. VIAL President Sampath Merenchige expressed appreciation for the port’s willingness to provide timely operational solutions and flexibility in support of its members.

articles.summary: A new traffic overpass connecting Tvaika Street to Kundziņsala will open on November 1, 2026, alongside a new port checkpoint at 42 Uriekstes Street, designated Delta 17, to facilitate freight traffic to and from the Port of Riga’s territory on Kundziņsala. articles.body: A new traffic overpass connecting Tvaika Street to Kundziņsala will open on November 1, 2026, alongside a new port checkpoint at 42 Uriekstes Street, designated Delta 17, to facilitate freight traffic to and from the Port of Riga’s territory on Kundziņsala. The EUR 82.6 million infrastructure project has been carried out by the Riga City Council in cooperation with the Freeport of Riga Authority, co-financed through the EU Cohesion Fund, with EUR 23 million from a state budget grant, EUR 59.6 million from a state budget loan and EUR 4.5 million from EU Cohesion Fund contributions. From November 1, freight vehicles will have two round-the-clock options to access Kundziņsala: via the new overpass through the Delta 17 checkpoint at 42 Uriekstes Street, or via the existing checkpoint at 9 Uriekstes Street, designated Delta 1. This transitional arrangement will remain in effect until the end of 2026. From January 1, 2027, the Delta 1 checkpoint at 9 Uriekstes Street will close to Kundziņsala-bound traffic, with all freight routed exclusively through the new overpass via Delta 17. Port terminal employees working on the island will be able to access Kundziņsala via the new overpass or through the existing Aptiekas Street route via the Delta 3 checkpoint at 36 Kundziņsala 3rd Line, open on workdays from 6:00am to 8:00pm, with prior coordination required for construction site access. The new overpass is fully accessible to residents of surrounding neighbourhoods, featuring an additional turning lane for vehicles travelling to and from the Kundziņsala residential area, a new pedestrian and bicycle path with lighting and dedicated runner lane markings, and three stair-equipped ramps on Tvaika Street and Kundziņsala. Freight carriers should note that while the new border crossing facility remains under construction, border inspection, customs control and food safety inspection services will continue to operate at 16 Uriekstes Street, with ionising radiation scanning for road cargo conducted at the Delta 17 address.

articles.title: From Ports to Power Plants: Decision Intel Transforms Critical Infrastructure
articles.summary: Critical infrastructure has never been more connected. Across ports, energy networks and industrial facilities, operators have access to unprecedented volumes of operational data generated by sensors, surveillance systems, satellite imagery, connected equipment and digital monitoring platforms.
articles.body: From Ports to Power Plants: Decision Intel Transforms Critical Infrastructure Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. By Dr. Chaouki Kasmi, CIO, Technology Innovation Institute (TII) October 19, 2026 © enanuchit/AdobeStock Critical infrastructure has never been more connected. Across ports, energy networks and industrial facilities, operators have access to unprecedented volumes of operational data generated by sensors, surveillance systems, satellite imagery, connected equipment and digital monitoring platforms. Every day, these technologies provide valuable insights into the performance, condition and security of critical assets. Yet despite this growing visibility, one challenge continues to persist. The problem is no longer collecting operational data. It is understanding what matters quickly enough to anticipate emerging risks, minimize disruption and make informed operational decisions. For years, investment in critical infrastructure has focused on expanding monitoring capabilities. More sensors, more connected devices and more operational systems have improved visibility across increasingly complex environments. While these technologies remain essential, they have also introduced a new challenge. Operators are often required to interpret fragmented information spread across multiple systems while responding to rapidly evolving operational conditions. In this environment, visibility alone is no longer enough. Whether managing a busy port, overseeing an energy network or monitoring geographically dispersed infrastructure, operators must bring together information from numerous sources before they can assess a situation and determine the appropriate course of action. Without that context, seemingly isolated operational signals can quickly develop into costly disruptions affecting supply chains, energy delivery and essential services. This challenge is remarkably consistent across critical infrastructure sectors. A modern port may simultaneously monitor vessel movements, cargo operations, weather conditions, perimeter security and logistics activity. Likewise, energy operators oversee extensive networks of pipelines, substations, generation assets and transmission infrastructure while monitoring environmental conditions, equipment performance and operational risks. Although these environments appear very different, they share a common operational reality: multiple systems generating vast amounts of information that must be interpreted together rather than in isolation, the conversation is therefore beginning to shift. Rather than asking how organizations can collect more information, infrastructure operators are increasingly asking how they can transform existing information into better operational decisions and, more importantly, identify risks before they escalate into operational incidents. This is where decision intelligence is emerging as a critical capability. Unlike traditional monitoring platforms, decision intelligence is designed to connect information across multiple operational domains rather than presenting individual data streams independently. By combining information from satellite imagery, geospatial intelligence, operational sensors, maritime systems, infrastructure monitoring and other data sources, it helps organizations develop a more complete understanding of complex operational environments. The objective is not simply greater visibility. It is greater understanding that enables organizations to recognize emerging risks earlier, respond proactively and strengthen operational resilience before disruption occurs. Artificial intelligence plays an important role in enabling this transition. Rather than replacing existing operational systems, AI acts as the intelligence layer that identifies relationships between multiple data sources, highlights emerging risks and provides operators with the context needed to prioritize decisions. By recognizing early indicators of operational change, organizations can move beyond reacting to incidents and instead anticipate them. For ports, this could mean combining vessel movements, weather data, satellite imagery and operational activity to improve maritime awareness, anticipate congestion or operational bottlenecks and minimize disruption across port operations. For energy operators, it could involve correlating infrastructure performance, environmental conditions, geospatial information and operational data to identify early indicators of equipment failure or operational risk before they affect service continuity. In both cases, the challenge is fundamentally the same. Operational decisions depend not on the quantity of information available, but on the ability to interpret it within the right context. This principle underpins TACTICAAI ’s approach to decision intelligence. By combining Earth Observation, geospatial intelligence, operational data, multi-sensor fusion and AI-powered reasoning, the platform is designed to provide operators with a common operational picture that supports faster, more informed decision-making. Rather than functioning as another monitoring platform, it enables organizations to connect fragmented information, understand developing situations and coordinate action across complex operational environments while helping anticipate and mitigate operational risks. Importantly, this approach does not replace human expertise. Operators remain central to every operational decision. AI supports that expertise by reducing cognitive workload, identifying relationships that may otherwise go unnoticed and presenting information in a way that enables faster interpretation. Human judgement continues to determine priorities, assess risk and make final decisions. As critical infrastructure continues to become more interconnected, the organizations that perform most effectively will not necessarily be those with access to the largest number of sensors or the greatest volume of operational data. Their advantage will come from recognizing emerging risks sooner, responding before disruption occurs and building more resilient infrastructure capable of adapting to increasingly complex operational environments. The future of critical infrastructure will not be defined by the volume of operational data organizations collect, but by how effectively they transform that data into decision intelligence, connecting information across domains, providing context for human operators and enabling organizations to anticipate risk, strengthen resilience and make better decisions. articles.title: Recent Changes in U.S. At-Sea Interdiction of Illicit Narcotics
articles.summary: Sometime back in the fall of 2025, I was contacted by a prominent national television, radio, and print news reporter with a surprising (but understandable under the circumstances) request for background information to inform her reporting.
articles.body: Recent Changes in U.S. At-Sea Interdiction of Illicit Narcotics Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Jeffrey Lewis , Contributor Jeffrey Lewis is a member at Cozen O’Connor and has over 30 years of extensive... October 19, 2026 Crewmembers from Coast Guard Station South Padre Island practice interdiction techniques with a 33-foot high-speed law enforcement boat and a 30-foot small boat. The station received three of these high-speed boats to enhance the unit's law enforcement capabilities. This style of 30-foot small boat is commonly used by drug smugglers and fishermen illegally dropping nets in U.S. waters. USCG photo by PA2 Adam Egger Sometime back in the fall of 2025, I was contacted by a prominent national television, radio, and print news reporter with a surprising (but understandable under the circumstances) request for background information to inform her reporting. She was working on a story covering the numerous lethal military strikes on alleged drug trafficking speedboats (lanchas) in international waters and the waters of Central and South American countries that we all were seeing and hearing about in the news. The reporter’s core question for me? Paraphrasing: We see how the military is conducting these operations now; how did it work before? It was and is an excellent question we all should be asking and the answers to which we as Americans all ought to know and remember, lest our society fall victim to the all-too-human phenomenon of “shifting baselines” — a dynamic akin to relative course plotting, in which we forget where we’ve been and how things once were done because we are only paying attention to what is happening in our immediate vicinity. Not long after my conversation with the reporter, the federal government started seizing oil-laden tank ships departing Venezuela and, not long after that, attacking the Islamic Republic of Iran, predictably grinding commercial transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz to a halt. And so it was that the lancha strikes seemed to be eclipsed by far more concerning events. As far as I can tell, the lancha strikes story I was interviewed for never made it to air or print (although others in the media have since refocused some attention on the issue). Still, I believe it is important to at least speak to the issue of how these military strikes are being executed now (from what little the American public is told) compared with how U.S. at-sea law enforcement interdiction efforts were previously conducted. In breaking this information down, I think the most easily digestible way to present it is with the familiar “Five W’s”: “ Who , What , Where , When , and Why ?” Who Conducts the Interdiction Operations? Historically, at-sea interdiction of illicit drugs has been a federal law enforcement mission conducted by the U.S. Coast Guard, and this is so for at least two important reasons. The first and most important reason is that the Coast Guard stands alone among the U.S. military services as both a branch of our military and a civilian law enforcement agency. Congress intentionally created it that way by statute (see 14 U.S.C. §§ 101 & 102). The other five services (Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force, Space Force) are subject to the Posse Comitatus Act (18 U.S.C. § 1385), under which they are expressly barred from civilian law enforcement activities. The second reason is that the at-sea interdiction mission—whether it be directed at illicit drugs or any other items smuggled into the United States—is at the core of the Coast Guard’s DNA. This goes back to its predecessor agency the Revenue Marine, which was conceived by our first Secretary of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton, and created by the 1st Congress of the United States on August 4, 1790, as a fleet of ten armed cutters that collected tariffs and deterred smuggling along the Atlantic Coast. Recently, beginning on September 1, 2025, the first of as many as 78 (reported numbers range from the 60s to the 70s) separate U.S. lancha strikes was reported in the news, with the most recent strike as of this writing reported to have occurred on September 19, 2026. Media reports are that the Trump administration is conducting these operations through the Department of Defense (DOD) military services, almost entirely with the use of aerial firepower. The deployment of military assets to strike these privately owned foreign boats is predicated on claims by the Trump Administration that the United States is in an armed conflict with Latin American drug cartels, and that the lanchas are carrying illicit cartel drugs bound for the United States. On this basis, the government appears to be justifying its actions as a lawful use of military force. However, a recent United Nations Human Rights Council report, released September 21, 2026, concludes the U.S. military strikes on lanchas are breaches of international law and could constitute crimes against humanity. What Are We Interdicting? Historically, we have always had a very good idea what kinds of contraband the Coast Guard is interdicting because they don’t just tell us, they show us. As a kid growing up on the Gulf Coast in the 1970s and 1980s, the image is burned into my mind of the Coast Guard captain and crew, just back from an enforcement operation, posing at the dock with bails upon bails of illicit narcotics confiscated at sea. It was in the local papers and on the nightly news shows every time you turned around. Those confiscated narcotics are critically important, because they are the key evidence that enables prosecutors to lock the drug smugglers away in prison for a long time. With the current lancha strikes, there typically is no evidence of what was onboard because in virtually every instance the entire boat, all its cargo, and most or all of its crew or passengers are blown to pieces in the water. We are told by DOD officials that there were illicit narcotics onboard, but little if any real evidence is offered to the public. We are expected to take the government at its word. Where & When Are We Conducting Drug Interdiction Operations? Again, owing to the traditional conception of narcotics interdiction viewed through a law enforcement lens, the Coast Guard typically (though not always) waits until a given drug smuggling vessel is in U.S. waters, because when it is in our waters, and particularly in our territorial sea or contiguous zone, not only are the Coast Guard’s law enforcement authorities at their zenith, but the vessel’s presence there is grounds for a reasonable suspicion that it is bound for the United States with whatever it has onboard. This is not to say that suspicion of a crime is necessary for an at-sea boarding—since 1790 the Coast Guard and its predecessors the Revenue Marine and Revenue Cutter Service have had the lawful authority to conduct suspicionless vessel boardings at-sea (see 14 U.S.C. § 522(a) and 19 U.S.C. § 1581(a)), and the courts have consistently upheld it as non-violative of our 4th Amendment right against unreasonable searches and seizures. The DOD lancha strikes since early September, 2025, have occurred largely in international waters of the Pacific and the Caribbean and, in a few instances, in the waters of other countries. Other than unsubstantiated claims by DOD officials that the boats are bound for the United States, there typically is no indication where they actually are headed. As a general matter, blowing up vessels transiting on the high seas raises serious concerns about violations by the United States of well-settled customary international law. The high seas are open to all countries and all vessels of those countries, which have a fundamental freedom of navigation under customary international law. Why Shift Emphasis from Coast Guard At-Sea Enforcement to Military Strikes on Lanches? Setting aside the apparent obsession with military lethality by some in the current administration and the penchant of others for inhumane cruelty (seemingly as some sort of deterrent), the only rational explanation for the change in approach to at-sea interdiction is that the new approach is more effective in stemming the tide of dangerous, illegal drugs coursing into the United States. Unfortunately, indications are that is not the case. According to a July 28, 2026, front page news story in the Washington Post, mid-year Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Pentagon reviews have concluded that the deadly military strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats have not reduced the amount of cocaine entering the United States. DEA analysts reportedly found that the lancha strikes have failed to affect the supply or price of cocaine in the United States and have led traffickers to diversify from lanchas in international waters—using different routes running in other countries waters and different means of transportation entirely, such as aircraft. Meanwhile the Pentagon reportedly has concluded that the lancha strikes have had no impact on the purity of illicit narcotics coming into our country. So all indications are we are not accomplishing the presumed goal of this new approach. In the meantime, on September 24, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security announced that the Coast Guard has exceeded 260,000 lbs. of cocaine seized in the Pacific since the start of its Operation Pacific Viper in August, 2025—an operation that appears to be employing all the traditional law enforcement tools described above. I think we are at a point with the DOD lancha strikes where we should be seriously asking ourselves whether the means justify the ends. Regardless, let us please not forget the way we traditionally have tackled this societal problem of illicit drugs and why—our commitment to the rule of law and equal justice under the law, and the reality that the world watches how the United States tackles difficult problems like this. We should be leading by example.
