articles.title: Dredging is Building the Next Generation of Northeast and Mid-Atlantic Ports
articles.summary: The United States’ Mid-Atlantic and Northeast regions have good dredging stories to tell. Major channel projects have been completed. Ports are investing in new capacity. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and its partners are advancing more work across the region.
articles.body: Dredging is Building the Next Generation of Northeast and Mid-Atlantic Ports Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. William Doyle , Contributor William P. Doyle is the CEO of the Dredging Contractors of America and the... October 19, 2026 The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) dredge MURDEN conducts maintenance dredging in the federal channel of the Ocean City Inlet, July 31, 2026. U.S. Army photo by David Adams The United States’ Mid-Atlantic and Northeast regions have good dredging stories to tell. Major channel projects have been completed. Ports are investing in new capacity. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and its partners are advancing more work across the region. At the same time, maintenance dredging keeps the channels that the private sector dredging industry built open for business. That progress is easy to see in Virginia. In February 2026, dredging was substantially completed on the Port of Virginia’s $450 million harbor and channel improvement project . The port now has a 55-foot-deep commercial shipping channel, the deepest on the East Coast (for now). Earlier widening work made room for two ultra-large container vessels to pass each other while in transit. These improvements give the largest ships in the Atlantic trade more flexibility to reach Virginia while fully loaded. This dredging also strengthens a major gateway that serves American exporters, importers and military vessels. It takes years to bring a project of that scale across the finish line. Congress must authorize the work. Federal and state partners must fund it. Engineers have to account for ship traffic, bridges, utilities, environmental requirements and where the dredged material will be placed. Dredging companies, including Manson Construction , The Dutra Group, Weeks Marine and other contractors executed portions of the deepening while ships kept moving in and out of the port. Cottrell Contracting has performed essential maintenance dredging in Norfolk Harbor’s inner channels. Virginia’s completed channel shows what long-term state planning, USACE partnering and private sector ingenuity can deliver. Boston Harbor offers another success. USACE, Massachusetts and Massport completed the $350 million Boston Harbor Deep Draft Navigation Improvement Project in 2022 , four months ahead of schedule. A joint venture of Cashman Dredging and The Dutra Group dredged approximately 11.7 million cubic yards of sediment and other material. Along with improvements at Conley Terminal, the deeper harbor has allowed larger container ships to call and helped expand Boston’s direct connections to overseas markets, including transatlantic service to Northern Europe and service to Asia via the expanded Panama Canal. Baltimore has major projects in motion. In May 2026, Tradepoint Atlantic and Terminal Investment Limited broke ground on the Sparrows Point Container Terminal at the former Bethlehem Steel site. The partners have committed approximately $1.2 billion in private financing. The planned 168-acre container terminal will have a 3,000-foot wharf, two berths and an on-dock rail yard. It is designed to handle two ultra-large container vessels at once and add more than one million containers of annual capacity. That is a major vote of confidence in Baltimore’s future. There is substantial dredging behind that investment. To give ships access to the new wharf, the existing Sparrows Point Channel and turning basin must be widened and deepened to 52 feet. The approved project calls for mechanical dredging of approximately 4.2 million cubic yards. That material has to go somewhere. The placement plan includes a new containment facility at High Head on Tradepoint property, existing Maryland Port Administration facilities at Cox Creek or Masonville, and suitable material transported to the Norfolk Ocean Disposal Site. The project secured its federal permit decision in December 2025. They’re not messing around and moving expeditiously. The DB Catalina, the largest mechanical dredge in the Western Hemisphere, conducts maintenance dredging operations at Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point, North Carolina. Photo Courtesy USACE The dredging is planned in stages as the terminal takes shape. Tradepoint’s construction schedule calls for an initial dredge cycle and construction of the High Head containment facility in 2026, followed by additional dredging and wharf construction in 2027. Maryland port officials reported in March that dredging associated with Sparrows Point was already underway, with more work scheduled. The planned first berth and rail yard are expected in 2028, followed by the second berth in 2029. This is a significant program of marine construction, not simply a new container yard on land. Elsewhere in Baltimore, Maryland and USACE are designing improvements to the loop channel serving Seagirt Marine Terminal . The plan would d eepen the West Seagirt Branch Channel to 50 feet and widen bends to improve vessel movements. Design is expected to be completed in late 2027. That channel dredging is still ahead, adding to the region’s longer-term pipeline. Baltimore also shows why dredged material placement must be planned years if not decades ahead of time. Poplar Island continues to receive material from navigation dredging while creating valuable habitat. With its available capacity filling over time, Maryland and USACE are building the next sites at Barren and James islands . The Mid-Chesapeake Bay Island Ecosystem Restoration Project is intended to provide capacity for 90 million to 95 million cubic yards of material over more than 30 years and restore more than 2,100 acres of habitat. Work is underway at both islands. The Corps’ fiscal 2026 work plan allocated $109.1 million to the Mid-Bay project, $22.5 million to Poplar Island and $76.69 million to Baltimore Harbor and Channels. This is how ports plan for continuing dredging while putting the material to productive use. On the Delaware River, the completed deepening of the main channel from 40 to 45 feet continues to pay dividends for ports in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. It also creates a lasting maintenance responsibility. In 2025, USACE awarded Norfolk Dredging Company a $27.6 million contract to maintain portions of the Delaware River and Wilmington Harbor channels. Maintaining the channel protects the value of the original investment and keeps ships moving reliably to terminals up and down the river. The next investment is already taking shape on the Wilmington waterfront. Delaware broke ground in September, 2026 on the Delaware Container Terminal at Edgemoor. The $669 million public and private project is designed for 45-foot berths and ships carrying up to 16,000 twenty-foot equivalent units. It is expected to open in 2029. Across the river system, Philadelphia is advancing SouthPort with a federal grant of more than $217 million for another berth and related improvements. These are terminal projects at different stages, but they point in the same direction. The region is preparing for more cargo, and dependable access to deep water will remain essential. The Port of New York and New Jersey is looking to its next chapter as well. Its 50-foot harbor deepening project was completed in 2016 after decades of work. Congress has since authorized improvements that include deepening selected federal channels to 55 feet. USACE and the Port Authority are now in preconstruction engineering and design. Construction of that larger program will require future funding and decisions. Its scale makes it one of the most significant long-term dredging prospects on the East Coast. In Connecticut, New Haven Harbor has taken an important step. USACE and the Connecticut Port Authority signed a project partnership agreement in April for improvements that include deepening the main channel, maneuvering area and turning basin from 35 to 40 feet. Congress authorized the project in 2020, and federal infrastructure funding is supporting its advance. It is another example of a regional port preparing to handle larger vessels more safely and efficiently. Dredging extends well beyond container, roll-on/roll-off and bulk ports and terminals. This year, USACE awarded beach nourishment contracts for several New Jersey communities, including Ocean City, Sea Isle City and Strathmere, and Avalon and Stone Harbor. The work will move sand from offshore areas to beaches and dunes. On Long Island, USACE plans to solicit a project to dredge Fire Island Inlet and place sand along Gilgo Beach. These jobs support coastal protection and restoration. The outlook is positive because the record is real. Virginia and Boston show what completed deepening can accomplish by a healthy and competitive private sector dredging industry. Baltimore and the Delaware River show the continuing importance of maintenance and dredged material management. New terminals, authorized channels and coastal projects offer substantial work ahead. We need steady funding, sound planning and timely project delivery to turn those opportunities into completed improvements. America’s dredging industry has the people, vessels and experience to get it done.

articles.summary: Congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration’s Jones Act waiver is growing, with Rep. Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) demanding answers about whether foreign vessels operating in domestic U.S. trades are complying with...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The Soho Square, a crude oil tanker sailing under the flag of Liberia, is at anchor in the Galveston Bay as it makes it’s way to the Port of Houston shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a 60-day waiver of the Jones Act shipping law, in Texas City, Texas, U.S. March 18, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian Congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration’s Jones Act waiver is growing, with Rep. Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) demanding answers about whether foreign vessels operating in domestic U.S. trades are complying with immigration, tax and maritime laws. In an October 16 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, first reported Monday by Bloomberg Government , Carbajal raised concerns about the administration’s oversight of the waiver, particularly following reports that foreign-flagged tankers had transported millions of dollars worth of petroleum products between U.S. ports without making required disclosures. The letter follows reporting by gCaptain in September that identified evidence of 14 previously unreported domestic tanker voyages, plus a possible 15th, expanding on an earlier Bloomberg Government investigation that found at least a dozen foreign vessels had moved more than $40 million in petroleum products without appearing in the Maritime Administration’s (MARAD) public waiver records. The missing voyages raised questions about how much foreign-vessel activity was actually taking place under the emergency waiver. A gCaptain review of MARAD’s September 16 data counted 255 reported movements under the original March 17 waiver and its May extension, but the additional voyages suggested that figure was incomplete. MARAD previously told Bloomberg Government that it lacks the legal authority to compel vessel operators to submit the required reports. Enforcement of the Jones Act falls to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which operates under DHS. Carbajal, the ranking Democrat on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee’s Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, is now seeking answers about whether other federal requirements are being enforced. “These reports raise significant questions about whether DHS and its component agencies are adequately enforcing federal law with respect to foreign vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce,” Carbajal wrote. One concern involves the immigration status of foreign seafarers working aboard vessels making domestic voyages. Federal immigration regulations generally prohibit foreign crewmembers admitted under D nonimmigrant status from working in connection with domestic vessel movements. Carbajal asked DHS and CBP to explain how they are applying that restriction to foreign officers and crewmembers aboard ships operating under the waiver, and what legal authority permits them to work on those voyages. He also requested information about any cases in which crewmembers were found to have immigration status inconsistent with domestic service, or had absconded from their vessels, along with any resulting enforcement actions. The letter also raises tax questions following recent Internal Revenue Service guidance clarifying that income earned by foreign corporations transporting cargo between U.S. ports under the waiver is considered domestic-source income and does not qualify for the international shipping income exclusion under Section 883 of the Internal Revenue Code or related treaty benefits. Carbajal wants to know whether DHS has coordinated with the Treasury Department and IRS to identify foreign vessel owners, operators and charterers using the waiver, including whether agencies have shared voyage dates, cargo movements and other information needed to determine potential tax obligations. He also requested details on DHS enforcement of other requirements covering maritime security, environmental protection, vessel safety and inspection, wages, labor and employment, customs and harbor maintenance. The latest questions come as the administration has tightened the waiver process. A second 90-day extension, which took effect August 17, requires operators to first submit a Vessel Availability Request so the government can determine whether a qualified U.S.-flagged vessel is available before authorizing foreign tonnage. Carbajal said publicly available information indicates that more than 25 domestic voyages have been completed under the current waiver, including multiple voyages by some vessels. The waiver was originally issued in March amid energy supply disruptions stemming from the war with Iran. The current extension runs through November 15. “The Administration has now authorized the waiver for an aggregate period of approximately 250 days, making oversight particularly important,” Carbajal wrote. “Congress has a responsibility to ensure that a national-defense waiver is not being treated as a broader exemption from federal law.” Carbajal requested a response by October 31, including details about coordination between DHS and the Departments of Defense, Transportation and Treasury, the IRS and Coast Guard. According to Bloomberg Government, DHS declined to comment and referred questions to the Department of Defense, which did not respond to a request for comment. articles.summary: U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24) has called on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to explain its oversight of Jones Act waivers following reports that foreign-flagged vessels transported more than $40 million in petroleum products between U.S.
articles.body: Carbajal Questions DHS Oversight of Jones Act Waivers, Foreign Vessel Ops Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 19, 2026 Copyright MarineLink.com | GT U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24) has called on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to explain its oversight of Jones Act waivers following reports that foreign-flagged vessels transported more than $40 million in petroleum products between U.S. ports without required disclosures. In an October 16 letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin , Carbajal, Ranking Member of the House Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, questioned whether foreign vessel operators benefiting from the waivers are complying with U.S. tax, immigration, labor and maritime regulations. "These reports raise significant questions about whether DHS and its component agencies are adequately enforcing federal law with respect to foreign vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce," Carbajal wrote. The Jones Act generally requires merchandise transported between U.S. ports to move aboard U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-documented vessels. Waivers issued under 46 U.S.C. § 501(a) permit exceptions when necessary for national defense. However, Carbajal emphasized that such waivers do not exempt foreign operators from other federal requirements. According to his letter, publicly available information indicates that foreign-flagged vessels have completed more than 25 domestic voyages under the current waiver, with some vessels making multiple trips. Carbajal also cited recent Internal Revenue Service guidance establishing that income earned by foreign corporations operating vessels between U.S. ports under Jones Act waivers constitutes domestic-source income and does not qualify for certain international shipping tax exemptions. His letter requests detailed information on four areas: federal tax compliance, immigration status of foreign crewmembers, enforcement of other maritime and labor regulations, and coordination among federal agencies. Particular attention is directed toward foreign mariners operating aboard vessels engaged in domestic transportation. Carbajal questioned how Customs and Border Protection interprets immigration restrictions applicable to nonimmigrant crewmembers and whether violations have been identified. He also requested information about coordination between DHS, the Departments of Defense, Transportation and Treasury, the IRS and the U.S. Coast Guard. "The Administration has now authorized the waiver for an aggregate period of approximately 250 days, making oversight particularly important," Carbajal wrote. "Congress has a responsibility to ensure that a national-defense waiver is not being treated as a broader exemption from federal law." Carbajal requested a DHS response by October 31, 2026. The inquiry follows letters he sent in June to vessel owners and operators benefiting from the Trump administration's waiver, seeking information about compliance with U.S. law and potential impacts on American maritime employment and domestic shipping capacity.

articles.body: C.H. Robinson has announced plans to appeal a US$604 million judgment in a trucking accident lawsuit, raising concerns about the legal responsibilities of freight brokers in the United States. The case, Lipe v. Lupus Superior , stems from a 2021 accident in which a truck struck stopped traffic, killing three people and the truck driver. A jury found the driver, trucking company Lupus Superior and C.H. Robinson liable. The judge has since upheld the verdict. C.H. Robinson disputes the ruling and maintains that it acted responsibly when selecting the carrier. C.H. Robinson disputes liability ruling The logistics company said Lupus Superior was an independent carrier with a Satisfactory safety rating from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA). According to C.H. Robinson, the carrier had completed nearly 270 shipments for its customers without incident before the accident. The company also stressed that it did not employ or supervise the driver involved. “We strongly disagree with the judgment in Lipe v. Lupus Superior and the misinformation presented at trial, and we remain confident in our appeal,” said Dorothy Capers, Chief Legal Officer at C.H. Robinson. The company maintains that the judgment does not establish the amount it may ultimately have to pay. The financial award could be overturned, reduced or modified during the appeals process. Freight broker safety standards under scrutiny Beyond the individual case, C.H. Robinson has called for clearer federal rules governing how freight brokers select trucking companies. The company argues that differing interpretations of carrier safety requirements across US courts create uncertainty for brokers, transport operators and shippers. It has urged Congress and federal regulators to establish a national carrier-selection safety standard. C.H. Robinson warned that continued legal uncertainty could discourage brokers from working with smaller trucking companies, potentially reducing available capacity and increasing transportation costs. The company said its business strategy and operating model remain unchanged while it pursues the appeal.

articles.title: DHL Group raises 2026 earnings outlook after strong third quarter

articles.body: DHL Group has raised its full-year 2026 earnings forecast following strong third-quarter results, supported by higher demand and improved profitability across its logistics operations. The company now expects Group earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to exceed €7 billion, up from its previous forecast of more than €6.5 billion. The revised outlook reflects stronger earnings momentum, particularly in DHL Express, alongside expectations of a robust seasonal peak in the fourth quarter. Third-quarter revenue and earnings increase DHL Group reported preliminary third-quarter revenue of approximately €22.6 billion, an increase of more than 12% compared with the same period last year. Group EBIT rose by around 16% to €1.71 billion, compared with €1.48 billion in the third quarter of 2025. DHL Express recorded EBIT of approximately €1.04 billion, up from €692 million a year earlier. The improvement was supported by pricing and cost measures, higher shipment weights and operating efficiencies. The division also benefited by around €100 million from capacity constraints in the air freight market. DHL Global Forwarding increased EBIT to approximately €260 million, compared with €195 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, DHL Supply Chain reported EBIT of around €300 million, up from €278 million in the corresponding quarter of 2025. DHL eCommerce recorded EBIT of approximately €50 million, compared with €176 million last year. The previous year’s figure included €123 million in positive non-recurring effects. DHL increases cash flow and investment forecasts Alongside its higher earnings outlook, DHL Group raised its full-year free cash flow forecast, excluding net mergers and acquisitions, to more than €3.2 billion. The previous estimate was approximately €3 billion. The company also increased its planned capital expenditure for 2026 to around €3.6 billion, from an earlier range of €3 billion to €3.3 billion. DHL said the additional investment would allow it to pursue selected growth opportunities. The Group expects combined EBIT from its DHL divisions to exceed €6.4 billion, compared with its previous forecast of more than €5.9 billion. Its outlook for Post & Parcel Germany remains unchanged at more than €900 million in EBIT. DHL Group will publish its full third-quarter financial report on November 5, 2026.

Join the leading maritime news network A view shows the Russian ice-class Arctic LNG carrier Nikolay Yevgenov is mangaed by Teekay, flagged Bahamas, and is classified by Russian Maritime Register of Shipping REUTERS/Stephane Mahe Oct 19 (Reuters) – Russia’s oil exports through its Northern Sea Route (NSR) in 2026 have already exceeded last year’s by nearly 50%, with some 20 million barrels shipped to Asia from the start of navigation in July to mid-October, traders said and data showed. The NSR links Russia’s western ports with Asian markets through icy Arctic waters and is considered a more dangerous and expensive route. This year, however, it became more attractive as a result of disruptions to routes via the Suez Canal, the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea area, traders said. Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, driving them to ?seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. This made high tariffs for ships using the NSR, which requires assistance from an icebreaker, less costly compared with the usual route to Asia through the Red Sea, traders said. For Russia, which controls the NSR, it represents a secure alternative to European waters, where tankers with its oil have been regularly arrested this year. The volume of Russian oil exported through the Arctic route is expected to rise by another 5-10 million barrels by the end of the navigation period, traders’ preliminary estimates show. Russia shipped 13 million barrels during the last navigation season. Gazprom Neft, one of Russia’s oil majors, will increase its shipments via the NSR by some 35% this year compared with 2025, its CEO Alexander Dyukov told journalists on Friday in Moscow. Russia also supplies significant volumes of LNG to Asia via the NSR as well as other goods. LNG supply via the NSR is also expected to rise this year after the launch of Arctic LNG shipments. President Vladimir Putin told an economic forum in Vladivostok in September that Russia expects cargo turnover via the NSR to double to 70 million metric tons annually by the end of the decade. Rosneft’s giant new oil project in the north of Russia, Vostok Oil, which opened last month, is already contributing to the rising volumes using the NSR. articles.summary: Iran’s main oil-loading terminals have remained empty for weeks, adding to signs that a US naval blockade of the country is throttling Tehran’s exports.

U.S. Central Command Photo (Bloomberg) — Iran’s main oil-loading terminals have remained empty for weeks, adding to signs that a US naval blockade of the country is throttling Tehran’s exports. No tankers have docked at Kharg Island’s crude-export terminals since late August, an analysis of ship-tracking data and European Union satellite images shows. That’s the longest stretch of inactivity at the island since the start of the US-Iran war in February. The lack of tankers at Kharg, deep inside the Persian Gulf, points to the increasing pressure on Iran since the US renewed its military blockade of the country’s shipping three months ago. Crude exports have plunged from almost 1 million barrels a day in July to nothing since late August, according to vessel-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg and figures from Kpler and Vortexa. July’s loadings were concentrated in the first half of the month, after a ceasefire deal between Washington and Tehran temporarily lifted the US blockade. No tankers laden with Iranian crude have managed to leave the country or nearby waters since the middle of that month, when the shipping ban was reimposed, nonprofit group United Against Nuclear Iran said. Iran exported nearly 650 million barrels of crude in the year through April, with most ending up in China, tanker-tracking data show. Now, as Tehran’s oil disappears from global markets, Chinese refiners are turning to other sources of crude and competing with other buyers for barrels and ships. That’s pushed oil prices higher and fueled a historic rally in freight. As Iran has been thwarted in its attempts to export its production, Tehran has stepped up attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the open seas. In the first two weeks of October, 25 ships were targeted in and around the chokepoint, compared with 18 incidents reported for the whole of September and 15 in August, according to alerts sent out by UK Maritime Trade Operations, a unit of the country’s navy. Kharg Island handles almost all of Iran’s crude exports, with Jask — a port at the eastern end of Hormuz — accounting for just a small percentage of the trade. While Kharg has been idle, no tankers have been seen berthed at Jask either, the satellite images show. The images reviewed by Bloomberg News were taken from the EU’s Sentinel 1 and 2 orbiters. They pass separately over the island every few days, and the longest gap between any of their images was three days. It typically takes about 24 to 48 hours to fully load a very large crude carrier at Kharg Island. A small ship appeared berthed on Oct. 10, seemingly breaking the 40-day period of dormancy. But its automated position signals identified it as the chemicals/products tanker Clavel, which has been shuttling between Iranian ports. Separately, at least two tankers were seen docked at jetties off Kharg Island’s southeast tip between Sept. 12 and Sept. 15, but those are only used to handle shipments of liquefied petroleum gas and sulfur. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The Trump administration has scheduled the first offshore mineral lease sale in U.S. history, opening more than 31 million acres of seabed near American Samoa to companies seeking critical minerals...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Polymetallic nodules, such as those shown here, can occur on the ocean floor and are of interest for the critical minerals they contain. Credit: NOAA. The Trump administration has scheduled the first offshore mineral lease sale in U.S. history, opening more than 31 million acres of seabed near American Samoa to companies seeking critical minerals from the deep ocean. The Department of the Interior’s Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) on Monday issued its Final Leasing Notice for the November 19 auction, clearing the final major administrative step before companies can bid on rights to explore and potentially develop mineral deposits on the U.S. Outer Continental Shelf. The sale, designated PACM-1, includes two lease areas covering approximately 31.5 million acres. The larger area encompasses 16.3 million acres, while the second covers 15.2 million acres. Under the final lease terms, each area carries a minimum bid of $3 million and a primary lease term of 20 years. Production royalties would begin at 2% for the first five years of commercial mining, increasing to 5% thereafter. The areas contain potential deposits of polymetallic nodules and ferromanganese crusts, which can hold valuable minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. The Trump administration has made expanding domestic supplies of critical minerals a national security priority, particularly as it seeks to reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains. “Critical minerals are no longer just commodities; they are a vital strategic asset in global competition,” said acting MMA Director Mike Olsen. Olsen said the agency also recognizes the cultural, economic and environmental importance of the waters surrounding American Samoa and would balance mineral development with environmental safeguards and engagement with local communities. Importantly, winning a lease would not immediately authorize mining. According to MMA, leaseholders would initially be permitted to conduct preliminary activities such as mapping and environmental surveys. More extensive exploration, testing and commercial mineral extraction would require separate federal approvals and environmental reviews. The agency has completed an environmental assessment of the leasing proposal and issued a finding of no significant impact for the initial activities. The announcement nevertheless drew sharp criticism from environmental groups, which have opposed opening the deep ocean to commercial mining before its ecological impacts are fully understood. “These lease sales will open the floodgates to the exploitation of our deep seas,” said Oceana Defense Campaign Manager Julia Singer. Singer accused the administration of disregarding opposition from scientists, local leaders and communities concerned about the potential environmental consequences. Oceana said the proposed lease areas are near Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a protected marine area that provides habitat for sea turtles, humpback whales and other species. Deep-sea mining could involve remotely operated machines collecting mineral-rich nodules from the seabed or removing crusts from underwater rock formations. Environmental groups warn that these operations could destroy seafloor habitats and create sediment plumes that affect marine life beyond the immediate mining sites. The leasing proposal has also raised concerns in American Samoa, where fisheries are a major part of the local economy. In comments submitted during the leasing process, American Samoa Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula called for stronger environmental monitoring, protections for tuna fisheries and greater oversight of vessels using Pago Pago Harbor. The governor also urged federal officials to consider the cumulative effects of mining-related vessel traffic, including potential pressure on port infrastructure, waste management and water quality. His comments emphasized that any future commercial extraction must be considered separately from the lease sale and should not be treated as an inevitable outcome. MMA said it had incorporated the governor’s recommendations where permitted by law or would address them during subsequent regulatory reviews. The governor also requested a share of federal mineral leasing revenues for American Samoa. In its response, MMA acknowledged that existing law does not currently provide authority for such revenue sharing. The latest announcement follows a series of steps by the Trump administration to establish a domestic offshore minerals industry. The government is also advancing a separate mineral leasing proposal near the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, while NOAA has been processing applications for deep-sea mineral exploration in international waters under U.S. law. MMA was established in July through the reunification of the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, bringing offshore leasing and safety oversight back under a single agency. The American Samoa auction is scheduled for November 19, with the final notice set for publication in the Federal Register on October 20. Whether the sale ultimately leads to commercial mining remains uncertain, but it marks a significant step in Washington’s effort to develop a U.S. deep-sea minerals industry. articles.title: Viking Yachts Tests AI Whale Detection Technology Aboard 70 Convertible
articles.summary: Viking Yacht Company is evaluating WhaleSpotter, an artificial intelligence (AI) whale detection system, aboard its new Viking 70 Convertible demonstration vessel. The technology uses thermal imaging and AI to identify whales ahead of moving vessels…
articles.body: Viking Yachts Tests AI Whale Detection Technology Aboard 70 Convertible Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 19, 2026 Whale-spotter on the tuna tower of a Viking 70, Image courtesy Viking Viking Yacht Company is evaluating WhaleSpotter, an artificial intelligence (AI) whale detection system, aboard its new Viking 70 Convertible demonstration vessel. The technology uses thermal imaging and AI to identify whales ahead of moving vessels, providing captains with advance warning to help prevent collisions. Installed by Viking subsidiary Atlantic Marine Electronics, the system features a thermal camera and processing computer mounted on the yacht's tuna tower. A tablet at the helm displays thermal imagery, estimated distance and bearing, while an audible alarm alerts the captain. According to WhaleSpotter, the technology can detect whales at distances of two to three nautical miles, day or night, depending on camera height and whale size. "Seeing a whale two or three miles ahead gives a captain time to make a small course correction to avoid it," said Shawn Henry, WhaleSpotter CEO. The system collected data during the yacht's recent transit from New Jersey to Florida, although no whales were detected. Viking will demonstrate the technology at the Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show, October 28 to November 1. The evaluation supports Viking's broader efforts to promote technology-based whale protection measures as NOAA considers modernizing its 2008 vessel speed rule, which limits most vessels 65 feet or longer to 10 knots in designated East Coast areas during specified periods. Since 2022, Viking's Whale and Vessel Safety (WAVS) Taskforce has evaluated whale avoidance technologies aboard a 24-foot Contender research vessel equipped with thermal imaging, radar and AI detection systems. "We're seeing tremendous progress in whale-detection technology, and these systems are becoming more practical and accessible for recreational boats," said John DePersenaire, Viking's Director of Government Affairs and Sustainability. Developed from research at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, WhaleSpotter reports more than 70 systems deployed worldwide aboard commercial vessels and at shore-based monitoring sites. L to R: Shawn Henry CEO of WhaleSpotter and John DePersenaire, Viking Director of Government Affairs and Sustainability. Image courtesy Viking

MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Courtesy of Eni A gas project off the coast of Libya, which is operated by Mellitah Oil & Gas Libyan Branch, a consortium formed by National Oil Corporation (NOC) of Libya and Eni North Africa, is anticipated to stop decades of costly flaring in its tracks, capturing hundreds of millions of cubic meters of gas to fuel local power plants and feed European export pipelines. Eni, in partnership with Libya’s National Oil Corporation through the joint venture Mellitah Oil & Gas, has announced the completion of the Bouri gas utilization project (GUP), with start-up procedures now underway, enabling the recovery of associated gas produced from the Bouri field in Libya’s western offshore area. The project involved the construction and installation of the new Bouri gas recovery module (GRM) and the related tie-in infrastructure, enabling the recovery and treatment of gas that was previously flared. The development is part of a broader strategy aimed at enhancing the value of the country’s gas resources while reducing the emissions intensity of upstream activities. According to Eni, this project represents one of the most significant emissions reduction initiatives in Libya’s energy sector and will contribute to improving the environmental performance of the country’s production system, reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by approximately 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year. The recovered gas will be supplied to the domestic market, providing an incremental production of around 700 million standard cubic meters per year, helping meet demand from the power generation sector. In addition, the project will support additional gas volumes available for export to Europe through the GreenStream pipeline. Saipem finished the lifting operations of the gas recovery module for the BGUP earlier this year. The pre-commissioning activities were planned for approximately 28 kilometers of already laid subsea pipelines to connect the DP3, DP4, and Sabratha platforms to enable the transportation of the recovered gas to the Mellitah treatment complex. articles.summary: The world's first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of green ammonia fuel, as China Energy Engineering Group (Energy China) describes it, has...
articles.body: Vessels October 19, 2026 · 15 hours ago 'World’s first' commercial ship-to-ship green ammonia bunkering performed in China NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email CMB.TECH The world's first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of green ammonia fuel, as China Energy Engineering Group (Energy China) describes it, has been completed in China. The operation was performed on October 13 at an anchorage in Zhoushan Port, Zhejiang Province, jointly by Energy China Hydrogen Energy, Belgium’s CMB.TECH and Jiangsu Andefu Energy Technology. From Energy China's HyFlow-1 Songyuan Hydrogen Energy Industrial Park project, a total of 1,000 tons of green ammonia was loaded through the dedicated liquid ammonia bunkering vessel Shenghang Yongle onto CMB.TECH's ammonia-powered ship, Mineral Europa . To make the ship-to-ship bunkering operation possible, Jiangsu Andefu Energy Technology obtained a liquid ammonia bunkering license from the Zhoushan municipal government in May, after which Shenghang Yongle completed its conversion for bunkering functions in August and was assigned the class notation “Ammonia Bunkering” by China Classification Society (CCS). Following bunkering, Mineral Europa will leave Zhoushan and cross the Pacific to Australia for commercial service. According to Energy China, the operation achieved several world firsts, including the first commercial ship-to-ship green ammonia bunkering at anchorage, the first dedicated ammonia bunkering vessel placed in service, and the first license for ship-to-ship liquid ammonia bunkering put into use. An arbitration panel has ruled that wage and other provisions previously agreed under the Oil Services Agreement between employers’ organisation Offshore Norge and trade union Styrke will also apply to the Well Services Agreement between Offshore Norge and SAFE. The decision ends a dispute that sparked a month-long strike and lockout over the summer before the parties agreed on July 14 to refer the matter to arbitration. The ruling covers changes to wage rates and union funds, with the new terms taking effect retrospectively from July 14 and remaining in force until May 31, 2028. SAFE expressed disappointment that the panel rejected its demand to maintain a separate agreement for members employed by SLB. However, the union welcomed the decision to backdate wage adjustments and other payments rather than apply them only from the date of the ruling. Despite the settlement, industrial unrest continues elsewhere in Norway’s offshore services sector. Reach Subsea confirmed that mediation with SAFE ended at midnight on October 16 without an agreement, prompting six offshore employees covered by the SAFE Offshore Collective Agreement to walk out on strike. The Haugesund-based company said it was assessing the operational and financial implications of the industrial action while staying focused on maintaining safe, efficient operations across its projects. Reach added that it remained committed to constructive dialogue with SAFE and finding a mutually acceptable solution as soon as possible. Norway’s national mediator confirmed that the parties remained too far apart for a settlement proposal likely to be accepted by both sides. The developments follow another wage settlement reached on Friday, when SAFE and Delta struck a deal with Offshore Norge and Norsk Industri over the separate Oil Agreement. articles.summary: The number of commercial transit voyages through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) had already surpassed the full-year 2025 total by the end of September, putting Arctic shipping on course for another record season as cargo volumes rise and more vessels test the route between Asia and Europe.

(Source: Atomflot) Cargo volumes rise as tanker, bulk carrier and container traffic expand, with 2026 transits potentially reaching 150. The number of commercial transit voyages through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) surpassed the full-year 2025 total by the end of September, putting Arctic shipping on course for another record season. The Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) identified 104 confirmed transit voyages through Sept. 30, compared with 103 during the entire 2025 navigation season and 97 in 2024 . Estimated transit cargo reached 3.7 million metric tons, up 15% from 3.2 million tons for all of 2025. The combined deadweight tonnage of vessels completing transits reached approximately 7.8 million tons, 26% higher than the 6.2 million tons recorded in 2025, according to CHNL’s analysis of AIS data from MarineTraffic by Kpler. The center estimates that the final 2026 total could approach 150 transits and exceed 4.5 million tons of cargo. Those figures remain provisional: as of Sept. 30, another 45 potential voyages were either underway or within the NSR area and could still qualify as completed transits. Tankers remained the largest cargo segment, with 22 eastbound voyages carrying an estimated 2.1 million tons, primarily crude oil. Murmansk was the main departure point, followed by Primorsk and Ust-Luga, highlighting the route’s role in moving Russian oil from Baltic ports toward Asian markets. Bulk carriers also recorded substantial activity. Thirteen eastbound voyages carried an estimated 1.1 million tons of cargo, while 27 westbound voyages reflected a significant repositioning of vessels toward the Baltic, Murmansk and other western destinations. The pattern underscores how the NSR serves not only as a cargo corridor but also as a seasonal route for moving commercial tonnage between operating regions. Container shipping offered another indication of the route’s evolving use. CHNL recorded 13 container ship transits by the end of September, including voyages between Asian and European ports that did not originate or terminate in Russia. Four international Asia-Europe transits had been completed, compared with just one during the entire 2025 season. Among them, the container ships Panstar Acro and Dubai Tower reached the United Kingdom from South Korea and China, respectively, while Riyadh Mukaab sailed from China to Felixstowe. The bulk carrier Nan Xin 27 completed a voyage from China to Klaipeda, Lithuania. Although still a small share of total NSR traffic, these voyages demonstrate growing interest in using the Arctic as an alternative Asia-Europe corridor. Ice conditions shaped the season’s development. During the first half of August, significant traffic diverted north of the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago , bypassing the conventional route through the Vilkitsky Strait. Conditions improved later in August, allowing traffic to return toward the traditional passage as open water expanded along the route. By early September, a more continuous open-water corridor had developed across much of the NSR. The late-season conditions were more favorable for continued navigation than in 2024 and 2025, when ice formation ended the navigation period early . Open-water conditions persisted beyond Sept. 30 this year, although seasonal freeze-up was expected to progressively restrict vessels without ice-class capabilities from mid-October onward. Photo: RasGas By Stephen Stapczynski Oct 19, 2026, (Bloomberg) –A carrier loaded with Qatari liquefied natural gas is sailing north through the Red Sea, potentially speeding up delivery to European customers with a rare transit through waters vulnerable to renewed attacks from Houthi rebels. The tanker, which loaded an LNG cargo in Qatar in August, is signaling Poland as its next destination, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Poland’s Orlen SA has a long-term supply contract with QatarEnergy, though shipments under the deal were canceled after the exporter’s giant Ras Laffan plant was hit by drone strikes in March. The transit — which comes as European natural gas prices hit the highest level in almost four years — is unusual. Commercial vessels have increasingly tended to take long detours to avoid the Red Sea, typically sailing around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to head to Europe, a route that can add almost two weeks and extra costs to a one-way journey. UK Maritime Trade Operations, a security outfit which links commercial shipping and military forces, reported on Saturday that an unnamed LNG tanker was approached southeast of the Yemeni port of Al Mukalla, in the Gulf of Aden, by a skiff that fired two shots. The tanker’s security team fired two shots in return. UKMTO did not provide further details, though ship-tracking data suggest the Poland-bound carrier was the only LNG tanker in the region at the time. The data suggests the vessel has since continued its journey. QatarEnergy did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
